Turn 1 of 4 — read-back. Do not write any program JSON in this turn.

You are going to turn a run-of-show into a Rhylthyme program: parallel **tracks** of sequential **steps**, each with a duration and a start trigger, that one person follows against a live clock.

Plan this as a Rhylthyme run-of-show and deliver a live timeline: Load-In Schedule — The Lyric for one-nighter, touring band, house crew of eight
Resource limits: one loading dock, one stage, one lighting desk, one PA, one monitor world, one green room.
Everything must be finished by doors.

Source text (read all of it):
<<<
Load-In Schedule — The Lyric, one-nighter

One loading dock, one stage, one lighting desk, one PA, one monitor world. Crew call is 8am and that is where this schedule starts. The dock takes one truck at a time, so the lighting truck empties before the backline truck pulls in, and nothing goes up on stage while the dock is still moving through it.

Dock
Lighting truck in: bars, fixtures, cable, 60 minutes.
Backline truck in the moment the lighting truck is empty: 45 minutes.
Clear the dock and get the empties out; 15 minutes.

Lighting
Rig the bars as soon as the lighting truck is off the dock: 45 minutes on stage.
Focus from the desk once the rig is up: 60 minutes.
Build the cues after focus: 30 minutes if the plot is clean, up to 90 if it is not.
Strike the rig when the show is down: 60 minutes.

PA
Fly the PA as soon as the lighting truck is off the dock: 75 minutes.
Ring out the house: 20 minutes.

Monitors
Set monitor world once the backline truck is off the dock: 45 minutes.
Ring out the wedges: 20 minutes.

Band
Backline up as soon as the dock is clear of the second truck: 45 minutes on stage.
Soundcheck when the house and the wedges are both rung out: 60 minutes, drums first.
Band dinner after soundcheck: 60 minutes in the green room.

House
Set front of house from two hours in: 60 minutes, merch, bars, ushers.
Clean the house after the band go to dinner; 30 minutes.
Doors when the house manager calls them; 30 minutes of walk-up.
Show on stage once the house is in, and it runs as long as it runs.
Backline out fifteen minutes after the show is down: 45 minutes on the dock.

Notes
The dock is the first bottleneck and the stage is the second. Focus and cue-build both want the desk, so they are strictly sequential. Soundcheck is the only step in the day that waits on two separate departments at once.
>>>

Read all of it before you answer. Then say back, in one paragraph and in your own words: what is being made, for how many (or at what scale), by when, and under what constraints — equipment that exists only once, how many people are working, anything that has to be held, rested or ready at a particular moment. If the text you were given looks truncated, or points at a section that is not here, say so instead of filling the gap.

End your reply with the same read-back as JSON in a single ```json fenced block:

```json
{
  "summary": "one paragraph: what is being made, for how many, by when, under what constraints",
  "servesOrScale": "8 people",
  "deadline": "2026-11-26T18:00:00",
  "constraints": ["one oven", "two burners", "two cooks"]
}
```

## Read-back

We're building a live, crew-facing run-of-show for a single one-nighter at The Lyric — a touring band load-in, soundcheck, dinner break, doors and show — as a Rhylthyme timeline of parallel tracks (dock, lighting, PA, monitors, band, house) that a house crew of eight follows against one shared clock, with the whole pre-show block racing a single deadline: **doors**. What's being *made* is not a product but a schedule-shaped process: six departments working in parallel on one stage, where the constraints are all singletons — one loading dock, one stage, one lighting desk, one PA, one monitor world, one green room — so the day is a chain of serializations. The dock handles one truck at a time (lighting truck empties before the backline truck pulls in, 60 then 45 minutes, then 15 to clear), and nothing goes up on stage while the dock is still working, which makes the dock the first bottleneck and the stage the second. Off those two gates: rigging (45) then focus (60) then cue-build — a *variable* 30–90 minutes depending on whether the plot is clean — with focus and cue-build strictly sequential because both want the one desk; the PA flies (75) and rings out (20); monitor world is set (45) and wedges rung out (20); backline is up (45). **Soundcheck is the only step that waits on two departments at once** — house ring-out *and* wedge ring-out — then runs 60 minutes, drums first, after which the band is held in the green room for 60 minutes of dinner while the house is cleaned (30). Front of house is set from two hours in (60, merch/bars/ushers). Doors is *called by the house manager*, not clocked, and 30 minutes of walk-up follows; the show then runs **indefinite** — "as long as it runs" — so the rig strike (60) and backline-out (45 on the dock, starting 15 minutes after the show is down) sit *after* doors and cannot be bounded by that deadline.

Two gaps I will not paper over: **the source gives no date and no clock time for doors** — only an 8am crew call, so "finished by doors" is a manual trigger, not a timestamp. And the ordering rules stated in prose ("nothing goes up on stage while the dock is still moving through it") are dependencies I'll have to encode explicitly as triggers, since the text gives gates, not start times.

```json

  "summary": "A live load-in run-of-show for one one-nighter at The Lyric: a touring band load-in, rig, soundcheck, dinner, doors and show, executed by a house crew of eight against a shared clock, in six parallel departments (dock, lighting, PA, monitors, band, house). Everything must be finished by doors, which the house manager calls. The day is defined by six single-instance resources — one loading dock, one stage, one lighting desk, one PA, one monitor world, one green room — so the dock (one truck at a time: lighting 60m, then backline 45m, then 15m to clear) is the first bottleneck and the stage the second, and no stage work starts while the dock is occupied. Rigging (45m), focus (60m) and cue-build (a variable 30-90m) are forced sequential because focus and cue-build share the one desk; PA fly (75m) and ring-out (20m); monitors set (45m) and wedges rung (20m). Soundcheck is 60m and is the only step waiting on two departments at once, then the band is held for a 60m green-room dinner while the house is cleaned (30m); the rig strike (60m) and backline-out (45m on the dock) happen after the show, which runs indefinitely, so they are outside the doors deadline.",
```

## Model check (my words)

The unit of the program is the **track**: one sequential line of work — one department, one station, one machine — and two things that happen at the same time can never sit in the same track, because steps within a track run one after another and must not overlap. A **step** is a single piece of work with a name, one `task` (the thing it occupies), and exactly one duration kind: **fixed** (a known `seconds`), **variable** (with `minSeconds`/`maxSeconds`, and a `defaultSeconds` so planning has a number to use), or **indefinite** (it runs until a human ends it — right for a show that "runs as long as it runs"). Each step says when it starts via a **startTrigger**: `programStart` for t=0, `programStartOffset` to start at a wall-relative point like "two hours in", `afterStep` to chain off another step's end (the workhorse here), `afterStepWithBuffer` for a fixed gap such as "fifteen minutes after the show is down", `manual` for something a person calls — doors — and `compound`/`onAbort` for waits-on-several or failure paths. `stepId`s are **globally unique across the whole program**, not per track, because triggers (and `analyze_schedule`'s critical path) refer to them by name from anywhere. Every `task` a step claims must have a matching **resourceConstraints** entry, and it's that entry's `maxConcurrent` — 1 for our dock, stage, desk, PA, monitor world and green room — that stops two steps using the same single resource at once. Repeated work (n trays, n samples, n trucks) is **one step with `replicates: {count, mode, maxInFlight}`**, never copy-pasted steps: `"each"` on the following trigger gives the downstream work one instance per repetition, `"all"` is the barrier that waits for every instance, and `maxInFlight: k` holds the *upstream* step back when the holding area between them only fits k — here the one-truck dock is exactly that kind of "hold the last truck, don't strand it" limit.

## Resource constraints I expect

Only one thing about this day is genuinely serial: the dock. Its steps (`lighting truck in` 60m, `backline truck in` 45m, `clear the dock` 15m, and `backline out` 45m at the end) must never overlap, so **`dock` = 1**. The source calls the stage its second bottleneck, so I'll declare **`stage` = 1** for the work that physically occupies the deck — rigging the bars, backline up, soundcheck, the show, the strike. Two things to flag rather than hide: (a) I am putting *flying the PA* under the **`pa`** task, not `stage`, because the step is literally assembling and ringing the PA system — if you'd rather every physical on-stage activity contend for the one stage, moving it to `stage` serializes rig-then-fly and pushes the whole afternoon later; (b) the text also says "nothing goes up on stage while the dock is still moving through it", which flatly contradicts the specific gates it then gives ("rig as soon as the lighting truck is off the dock" at t=60, while the backline truck is still on the dock until t=105) — I'm following the specific per-department gates and treating the general line as intent, not a hard rule. The **`lightingDesk`** is 1 and is what forces focus then cue-build strictly sequential, because both want that desk even though they're different steps. **`pa` = 1** covers fly-the-PA and ring-out-the-house; **`monitorWorld` = 1** covers setting monitor world and ringing out the wedges. **`greenRoom` = 1** holds the band for the 60-minute dinner — a hold, not work, but the same room can't be anything else meanwhile. Finally I need one entry the source's resource list never names but the validator requires, because "set front of house" and "clean the house" are steps that must belong to *something*: **`house` = 1** (merch/bars/ushers setup, then the post-dinner clean, then the 30-minute walk-up). On headcount: the text gives me exactly one number — eight people, crew call 8am — and no split by department, so I'm declaring `actors: 8` globally and **refusing to invent per-department headcounts**; if those eight are one shared pool rather than six separately-staffed departments, the dock, rig, PA fly, monitor set and FOH set are all running concurrently around t=60–150 and a `crew` constraint would be the real binding limit — worth resolving before the extraction turn. Scope note on the deadline: the source supplies no date and no clock time for doors, only the 8am crew call and "doors when the house manager calls them", so `doors` will need a `manual` trigger and I'll treat the pre-show block as the thing that must be done by doors, with strike and backline-out sitting after it, unbounded.

```json
{
  "acknowledgement": "Tracks are sequential lines of work — one department or machine each, no overlapping steps inside a track, and anything simultaneous lives in a different track. Every step has exactly one duration kind: fixed (seconds), variable (minSeconds/maxSeconds/defaultSeconds) or indefinite (runs until a person ends it). Every step carries a startTrigger — programStart, programStartOffset, afterStep, afterStepWithBuffer, manual, onAbort or compound — which pins it to the clock, to another step, or to a human call. stepIds are unique across the WHOLE program, not per track, because triggers reference them by name from anywhere. Every task a step occupies needs a matching resourceConstraints entry, and its maxConcurrent is what stops two steps sharing one dock, one stage, one desk, one PA, one monitor world or one green room. Repeated work is one step with replicates {count, mode}, chained downstream with instances:'each', barrier'd with instances:'all', and held back with maxInFlight:k when the space between repetitions is the real limit.",
  "resourceConstraints": [
    { "task": "dock", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "stage", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "lightingDesk", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "pa", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "monitorWorld", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "greenRoom", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "house", "maxConcurrent": 1 }
  ],
  "actors": 8
}
```

## Extraction — every timed activity, in text order

Walking through the text as if I were the one doing the day, I get **19 timed activities**. Three judgment calls to flag up front, since they're mine, not the text's:

1. **"Build the cues after focus: 30 minutes if the plot is clean, up to 90 if it is not"** is the day's only genuinely uncertain work, so it's the only `variable`: 1800–5400 s. I'm setting `defaultSeconds` to **1800**, the clean-plot case the text leads with, purely as the planning number — if this were a must-hit-doors plan I'd want 3600 (midpoint) or 5400.
2. **Task assignment where a step touches several singleton resources.** `soundcheck` occupies the stage but *waits on* PA and monitor world — I've given it `task: "stage"` and will express the two-department dependency as a `compound` trigger next turn, not as a resource claim. Same reasoning for `strike-rig`: it's the physical rig coming off the deck, so `stage`, not `lightingDesk`.
3. **The 15-minute post-show gap and the "from two hours in" start are not activities** — no work happens in them. They belong in triggers (`afterStepWithBuffer`, `programStartOffset`), so I've deliberately left them out of this list, and `backline-out` appears here as the 45-minute dock job alone.

**No inferred steps.** I looked for the preheat-equivalent and there isn't one: every rest, hold and gap in this text is either a stated duration (clear the dock, dinner) or a pure wait (the 15 minutes, the two-hours-in start). Two candidates I considered and rejected: a separate "power and patch the desk" step (the text's focus already "from the desk", so it would be invention), and splitting soundcheck into "drums" then "rest of band" ("drums first" gives an internal order but only one duration, so it stays one step).

Also noted, not resolved here: "nothing goes up on stage while the dock is still moving through it" contradicts the specific gates that follow (rig and fly both start when the *lighting* truck is off the dock, at 60 min, while the backline truck is still on it until 105 min).
